title: Act III: ALSEP Deployment & Nuclear Power on the Moon

lines.speaker: David Scott
lines.text: We are roughly 110 meters west-northwest of Falcon, clear of any ascent engine blast zone. Jim, let's unpack the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package.

lines.speaker: James Irwin
lines.text: Central Station box is on the ground. Opening the sunshields and aligning the helical transmitter antenna toward Earth. Frequency will downlink at 2278.0 MHz.

lines.speaker: David Scott
lines.text: Now for our power plant: the SNAP-27 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator. I have the fueling tool in hand. Unlatching the graphite cask on the descent stage.

lines.speaker: James Irwin
lines.text: Careful, Dave. That four-kilogram fuel capsule of Plutonium-238 is glowing with radioactive thermal decay. Half-life is 89.6 years.

lines.speaker: David Scott
lines.text: Sliding the rod smoothly into the RTG's central cylinder... latched and locked! Those 442 lead-telluride thermocouples will convert that natural heat straight into 70 Watts of clean DC power.

lines.speaker: James Irwin
lines.text: No batteries to freeze during the brutal fourteen-day lunar night. This little nuclear generator will keep ALSEP sending data back to Earth for years to come.

lines.speaker: David Scott
lines.text: Let's emplace the experiment suite around the station. I'm unreeling the ribbon cable for the Passive Seismometer.

lines.speaker: James Irwin
lines.text: Seismometer leveled and covered with the Mylar thermal shroud. It's sensitive enough to detect moonquakes, thermal tremors, and even our LM ascent stage when we crash it later to map the lunar interior.

lines.speaker: David Scott
lines.text: I'm deploying the Lunar Surface Magnetometer at the end of its 15-meter cable. Its three fluxgate sensors will measure the local magnetic field and see if the Moon has an iron core.

lines.speaker: James Irwin
lines.text: Here goes the Suprathermal Ion Detector and Cold Cathode Ion Gauge. They'll measure positive solar ions and detect any trace atmospheric gases hovering above the surface.

lines.speaker: David Scott
lines.text: And the Solar Wind Spectrometer is pointing up, measuring protons and electrons flowing straight from the Sun. Now, I have to tackle the Apollo Lunar Surface Drill for the Heat Flow Experiment.

lines.speaker: James Irwin
lines.text: That regolith gets dense fast, Dave. Watch your heart rate on the drill.

lines.speaker: David Scott
lines.text: Pushing through... the flutes are clearing cuttings. Probe one is down! These sensors will measure the rate of geothermal heat leaking out from the Moon's primordial core.

lines.speaker: Joe Allen (CAPCOM)
lines.text: Falcon, Houston ALSEP station confirms: Central Station received initial power commands at 18:37 UT. Telemetry looks rock-solid across all seven science packages. Tremendous work, gentlemen!
